seo_title: Wendigo: the real Algonquian legend, history and the antlered myth
seo_desc: What the wendigo actually is in Cree, Ojibwe and Innu tradition, where the word comes from, the Swift Runner and Jack Fiddler cases, wendigo psychosis, and how horror movies gave it antlers.
summary: A being of winter, hunger and greed from Algonquian traditions, a long way from the antlered horror-movie version.
body: The wendigo comes from the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples in the northern forests of Canada and around the Great Lakes, including the Ojibwe, Cree, Saulteaux, Naskapi and Innu. In those teachings it's tied to winter, cold and starvation, and to a greed that can never be filled. It's also a moral idea, a warning about what selfishness does to a person and to the people around them.

These are living traditions, and a lot of Indigenous people would rather the wendigo wasn't treated as a campfire monster, so I've tried to keep this page to what the traditions and the historical record actually say. The deer-skulled, antlered thing from movies and games is a modern invention and it gets its own section below.

p: The English word is a borrowing from two Algonquian languages, the Cree wīhtikōw and the Ojibwe wiindigoo. It's been showing up in English writing in one spelling or another since at least 1714, when it was written down as Whitego. You'll also see windigo, witiko and wetiko. The "wendigo" spelling most people use now was made popular by the English writer Algernon Blackwood, who published a novella called The Wendigo in 1910.

Descriptions vary from nation to nation but the core is the same. The wendigo is a cannibal spirit or being of the north, and it's linked to winter and famine. Ojibwe scholar Basil Johnston wrote that it was gaunt to the point of starving, with skin pulled tight over its bones, an ash-grey colour, eyes sunk deep in its head and torn, bloody lips, and that it gave off a smell of decay.

In Ojibwe, Eastern Cree, Naskapi and Innu stories it's often a giant many times bigger than a person. Every time it eats someone it grows to match the meal, so it can never be full. That's the whole point of it really. It's hunger and greed that only get worse the more they're fed.

Some teachings say a person overtaken by greed can turn into a wendigo, and others say it happens to someone who resorts to eating human flesh to survive. Either way the lesson is about taking care of each other in a hard winter instead of looking out for yourself.

Among the Assiniboine, Cree and Ojibwe there was a ceremonial dance, wiindigookaanzhimowin, held in times of famine to remind people how serious the taboo was. Dancers wore masks and danced backward around a drum. The last one known in the United States was held at Lake Windigo on Star Island in Cass Lake, on the Leech Lake Reservation in northern Minnesota.
Two real cases from western and northern Canada come up any time people talk about the wendigo, and both are sad stories more than scary ones.

In the winter of 1878 to 1879 a Cree man in what's now Alberta named Swift Runner killed and ate members of his family, including his wife and children, even though a Hudson's Bay Company post with emergency food was only about 25 miles away. Because food was that close, it wasn't treated as survival cannibalism, and he's often described as having believed he was possessed by a wendigo. He was hanged at Fort Saskatchewan in December 1879.

Jack Fiddler was an Anishinaabe leader and medicine man from the upper Severn River in northwestern Ontario. He was known for protecting his people from the wendigo and claimed to have defeated fourteen of them, which sometimes meant ending the life of a very sick person before they turned, at the family's request. In 1907 the North-West Mounted Police arrested Jack and his brother Joseph for the killing of Joseph's daughter-in-law, Wahsakapeequay, the year before. Jack got away from his guards on September 30, 1907 and took his own life. Joseph was convicted, and the order releasing him came three days after he died in custody in 1909. Their arrest is basically the point where Canadian law was forced onto a people who had lived by their own law until then.

Western doctors and anthropologists later turned the stories into a diagnosis called "wendigo psychosis", described as an overwhelming craving for human flesh and a fear of becoming a cannibal. It ended up listed as a culture-bound syndrome.

A lot of researchers don't buy it. In 1982 anthropologist Lou Marano argued in the journal Current Anthropology that nobody had ever actually studied a real case, and that many of the people labelled as wendigos were really people accused by their communities in very hard times. Even the medical listings now mention that its legitimacy is in question. For what it's worth I think Marano makes the stronger case.

sections.h: How the movies gave it antlers
p: Here's where the version most people know comes from. Blackwood's 1910 novella turned the wendigo into a horror monster for English readers. August Derleth's Ithaqua stories in the 1930s and 40s built on that, and Stephen King used the idea in Pet Sematary (1983). Marvel Comics added a wendigo in The Incredible Hulk #162 in 1973, which looked more like a white-haired Bigfoot than anything from the traditions.

The deer skull and antlers don't come from Cree or Ojibwe teachings at all. That look built up through horror art, video games like Until Dawn (2015) and online stories, and the 2021 film Antlers, produced by Guillermo del Toro, pretty much locked it in. So if you see an antlered skeleton creature called a wendigo, that's the pop culture version.

Indigenous writers have taken the idea back on their own terms too. Louise Erdrich's National Book Award winner The Round House and Linda Hogan's Solar Storms both use the wendigo, and "wetiko" is used by some Indigenous thinkers as a word for greed and for colonialism itself.

faq.a: In the traditions of Algonquian-speaking peoples like the Cree, Ojibwe and Innu, the wendigo is a cannibal being or spirit of the northern winter, tied to starvation and to greed that can never be satisfied. It's both a creature in stories and a warning about selfishness.

It's a spiritual and moral figure from living Indigenous traditions, not an animal anyone has found. There are real historical cases linked to wendigo beliefs, like Swift Runner in 1879 and Jack Fiddler in 1907, but those are about people, famine and belief.

faq.q: Why does the wendigo have antlers?
faq.a: It doesn't in the traditions. The antlers and deer skull are a modern horror invention that grew out of books, games and films, and the 2021 movie Antlers made that look famous.
The word comes from the Cree wīhtikōw and the Ojibwe wiindigoo. It's been written in English since at least 1714 and the spelling "wendigo" caught on after Algernon Blackwood's 1910 story.

It's a label Western psychiatry gave to cases of people said to crave human flesh or fear turning into a wendigo. Many researchers, including anthropologist Lou Marano in 1982, argue it was never properly documented and doesn't hold up.

faq.q: What is the difference between a wendigo and a skinwalker?
faq.a: They come from completely different peoples and parts of North America. The wendigo is from northern Algonquian traditions in Canada and the Great Lakes and is about hunger and winter. The [skinwalker](/creatures/skinwalker/) comes from Navajo (Diné) tradition in the US Southwest.
